items.prose: A coin lands heads with chance 0.6. It is coded with a code built for a fair coin.
items.question: What is the cross-entropy, in bits per toss?

feedback.correct: Every word of the fair code is 1 bit, so the average is 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Weigh $-\log_2 0.5$ by the true chances.

byKey.entropy: That is $H(0.6, 0.4)$, the cost of the right code.

items.question: What is $D(p \| q)$, in bits? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out $\sum p \log_2(p/q)$; one term is negative.

byKey.abs: You added the sizes of the terms. The first is negative.

items.prose: The proof that $D(p \| q) \ge 0$ uses $E_p[\log_2 \tfrac{q}{p}] \le \log_2 E_p[\tfrac{q}{p}]$.
items.question: Why does that step hold?

options.why: For a convex $g$ Jensen gives $\ge$. $\log_2$ is concave.
Increasing is used at the last step, $\log_2 \sum q_i \le \log_2 1$. This step needs concavity.

feedback.correct: Concavity: chords of $\log_2$ lie below its curve.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which shape does $\log_2$ have?

explain.text: For a concave $g$, $E[g(X)] \le g(E[X])$. Here $g = \log_2$ and $X = q/p$ under $p$.

items.prose: A model's held-out loss is 4.5 bits a token.
items.question: What is its perplexity? Give a decimal to 1 place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Raise 2 to the loss in bits.

byKey.e: That is $e^{4.5}$. The loss is in bits.

items.prose: A model's held-out loss is 1.8 nats a token.
items.question: What is its perplexity? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. With nats, raise $e$ to the loss.

explain.text: $e^{1.8} \approx 6.05$: like a fair choice among about six tokens.

items.prose: A share rose on 11 of 20 days. A constant forecast $\theta$ is fitted by least average negative log-likelihood.
items.question: What is the least average loss, in bits per day? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The least loss is the entropy of the data's shares.

byKey.fair: That is the fair forecast. The fitted one does a little better.

explain.text: The fit is $\hat\theta = 0.55$, and its loss is $0.55 \times 0.862 + 0.45 \times 1.152 \approx 0.993$ bits.

options.why: In $D(p \| q)$ the third term has weight $p_3 = 0$ and drops out.
$D(p \| q)$ skips the third outcome, where $p = 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find a zero in the second distribution under a positive weight.

explain.text: A divergence is infinite when the second distribution is 0 where the first is positive. Only $D(q \| p)$ has that: $p_3 = 0$ under $q_3 = 0.3$.

items.prose: Model A reports a held-out loss of 0.95 bits per symbol. Model B reports 0.68 nats per symbol on the same test set.
items.question: Which model is better?

options.why: The units differ. In bits B scores 0.981.
Same test set, same symbols: convert one unit and compare.

feedback.correct: In bits, B scores $0.68 / 0.6931 \approx 0.981$, above A's 0.95.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Put both in one unit first.

explain.text: $0.68 \text{ nats} = 0.68 \times 1.4427 \approx 0.981$ bits. A is lower, so A predicts the test set better.

items.question: What is it in nats? Give a decimal to 3 places.

byKey.bits: That is the figure in bits.

items.prose: A model scores a total negative log-likelihood of 412 nats on 500 test symbols. On a 100-symbol subset it scores 85 nats.
items.question: On which does it predict better per symbol?

options.text: The subset: 0.85 nats a symbol against 0.824
options.why: Per symbol, the full set is 0.824 and the subset 0.85: the full set is lower.

options.text: The full set: 0.824 nats a symbol against 0.85
The subset, because 85 is far below 412
options.why: Totals grow with the number of symbols. Divide first.

feedback.correct: $412 / 500 = 0.824$ and $85 / 100 = 0.85$: the full set is lower per symbol.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn both totals into averages.

explain.text: Averages compare and totals do not: 0.824 against 0.85 nats a symbol.
